ref: #cc-for-you > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a > div > img
subject: Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)
message: The text alternative "Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)" describes something the image does not show.
evidence: Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is a 32px vehicle icon inside the 'Mais Acessados' link to service 2671. The link also shows the same text, 'Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)', and the live HTML is unchanged. An image inside a link may take an alt that states the link's function, so 1.1.1 does not require the alt to describe the picture. The alt only repeats the visible text. alt="" would be better practice (H2), but that redundancy is not a 1.1.1 failure. The suggested 'Ícone de veículo' would add nothing useful.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is a 32x32 vehicle pictogram inside the 'Mais Acessados' link whose visible text is 'Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)'. Its alt names the service the icon stands for, which is a functional or symbolic alternative, and WCAG 1.1.1 asks for equivalent purpose, not a description of how the icon looks. The alt repeats the adjacent link text. That is a redundancy issue (H2 or alt="" would be cleaner), but it is not a 1.1.1 failure, and it is not the mismatch the finding claims. The suggested patch, 'Ícone de veículo', would make it worse. The live markup is unchanged.

subject: DAE para pagamento de IPVA - boleto/pix
message: The text alternative "DAE para pagamento de IPVA - boleto/pix" describes something the image does not show.
evidence: DAE para pagamento de IPVA - boleto/pix

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is a document-with-dollar-sign icon inside the link to service 2426. The visible link text, 'DAE para pagamento de IPVA - boleto/pix', is the same as the alt. The alt states the link's function, which is acceptable for an image inside a link. Repeating the visible text is a redundancy best-practice issue (H2 would use alt=""), not a failure of 1.1.1. skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is a 32x32 document-with-currency pictogram inside the link 'DAE para pagamento de IPVA - boleto/pix', and the link text is visible. The alt gives the purpose of the service the icon represents, which is acceptable under 1.1.1's equivalent-purpose requirement, and it duplicates the link text. That makes it redundant, but redundancy is not a failure. The finding requires the alt to describe the icon's appearance ('Ícone de documento com cifrão'), which is a rule WCAG does not impose and would degrade the link name.

skeptic.label: false_positive

The claim that the alt 'describes something the image does not show' applies an appearance-description rule that is stricter than, and different from, WCAG's.

ref: #cc-for-you > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > img
subject: Ceará em Destaque
message: The text alternative "Ceará em Destaque" describes something the image does not show.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the featured photo of the 'Ceará em Destaque' bulletin card (a buggy on a sand dune). It is not inside a link, and the h3 directly above it is also 'Ceará em Destaque'. The alt names the publication, not what the photo shows, and the live HTML is the same. If the photo is treated as informative, the alt does not convey its content and the finding holds. If it is an illustration in a card whose information is all in the heading, date and link, it is decorative and the alt is only redundant. That would be at most an F38-style issue, not the inaccurate description the finding claims. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree about whether this photo carries information.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the featured photo of the 'Ceará em Destaque' bulletin card: a buggy on a dune with a beach behind it. It sits directly under the h3 'Ceará em Destaque' and above 'Boletim publicado! 09/10/2026 / Ler boletim'. The image is not a link, and its alt repeats the h3. Competent auditors would split three ways. One reading treats it as an informative photo, so the alt fails as claimed. Another treats it as ambience next to its own heading, in which case the right fix is alt="" (an F38-style issue) rather than a description. A third treats it as the edition's cover image, which is fairly identified by the publication's title. The evidence cannot settle which purpose the photo serves.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'Banners institucionais' slide image. It is the only content of a link to the 'matérias especiais' news category, and the live HTML is unchanged. Its alt, 'Tarja-Especiais-Site-Interna-1', is the file name. The image is text: 'ESPECIAIS - Reportagens que vão além dos fatos cotidianos'. A file name used as alt is documented failure F30 of 1.1.1. Because the image is the link's only content, the link's purpose is lost as well (2.4.4).

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the first slide of the 'Banners institucionais' carousel and is visible at load. It is an image of text reading 'ESPECIAIS - Reportagens que vão além dos fatos cotidianos'. ref: #login-button-desktop
subject: Entrar
message: The text "Entrar" has at most 3.42:1 contrast with what is behind it (#fefefe on #22a33e…#1e9f41), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a gradient). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the desktop 'Entrar' outline button in the header: white text on the header's green gradient. Sampling the screenshot inside the button gives #21a23e to #24a53a behind #fefefe, about 3.2:1 to 3.4:1. At 20px and weight 400 the text is not large, so it needs 4.5:1, and it fails. The page has an 'Alternar alto contraste' toggle, but G174 does not rescue this. G174 requires the alternate presentation to meet all other criteria, and that mode would keep failures such as the file-name alt on the 'Especiais' banner. So 1.4.3 fails in the default view.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The measurement holds up. The 'Entrar' link in the header is #fefefe text on the green header gradient (about #20a13f behind it). style.css sets .btn-outline-cc to 1.25rem (20px) with font-weight 400 !important, so this is normal-size text needing 4.5:1, and it reaches only about 3.3-3.5:1 in the default presentation. The page, however, offers a visible, focusable 'Ativar alto contraste' toggle in the same header (its icon is about 3.8:1 against the green; it is also bound to Alt+Shift+C). Activating it sets body.contrast-active, and menu-mobile.css then forces the header to #111 with white text, which passes. This is technique G174. Whether that suffices is debatable: G174 needs the control itself to meet the contrast requirement, and it is an icon at 3.8:1, not text at 4.5:1. It also needs the alternate version to conform fully, which this page's other failures make doubtful. Auditors would reasonably disagree, so this is a true positive only if the toggle is not accepted.

ref: #cc-for-you > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > h4
subject: Boletim publicado!
message: The text "Boletim publicado!" has at most 2.86:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ef6000 on #dff0ee…#e8f0ef), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a pseudo-element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 3:1 for large text.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the h4 'Boletim publicado!' on the bulletin card, in .text-secondary orange. Sampling the screenshot gives text pixels of exactly #ef6000 on a pale mint gradient (#dff1ef to #e8efee), about 2.83:1. At 24px and weight 500 it counts as large text, so it needs only 3:1, but it still falls short. The live markup is unchanged. The high-contrast toggle does not excuse it, for the same G174 reason as the 'Entrar' button.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The measurement holds up. The h4 'Boletim publicado!' is 24px weight 500 in Kanit, which counts as large text needing 3:1. Its CSS colour is #ef6000 on the light gradient card band (#dff0ee to #e8f0ef), giving 2.81-2.86:1; my own pixel sample was at most 2.92:1. So the default presentation narrowly fails 1.4.3. The page does provide a high-contrast toggle (G174). In that mode, home-for-you.css sets this card band (.for-you-card--last-boletim .bg-active) to background #111 and .text-secondary/.titulo to #fff, which passes easily. Whether that toggle satisfies 1.4.3 is open to debate. Its icon is only about 3.8:1, and G174 requires the alternate version to conform fully, which is doubtful here. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree, so this is a true positive only if the toggle is not accepted.

ref: #header-institucional > div:nth-of-type(1) > nav > div:nth-of-type(2) > a > img
subject: Title
message: The text alternative "Title" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the 'SENADO FEDERAL' logo, the only content of a link to www.senado.leg.br. Its markup is inside . The browser's accessibility tree gives the link the name "Title" (from its contents); "Senado Federal" from the title attribute is only its description. The alt is placeholder text: it does not identify the logo or where the link goes, which is failure F30 / technique H30. The live page still has alt="Title". Rampa's snapshot shows the link name as "Senado Federal", which is wrong, but the finding's claim holds.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The header logo link (to www.senado.leg.br) holds only an img whose alt is "Title"; the image shows the text "SENADO FEDERAL". Chrome's AX tree gives the link the name "Title" (from contents), with the link's title attribute "Senado Federal" exposed only as a description. Rampa's own snapshot name "Senado Federal" is a naming error, but the claim stands. A placeholder alt like "Title" is not an equivalent for a functional logo image (F30). I found no technique that rescues it, and the live page is unchanged.

subject: Buscar

ref: #footer-institucional > div > footer > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > a:nth-of-type(1)
subject: ENGLISH
message: "ENGLISH" is in English, but it inherits the page's language (pt-br): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="en" to the link.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the footer language link "ENGLISH" (to the English Carta de Serviços), on a page with lang="pt-br" and no lang on the link. This is the "Alternative language links" example in Understanding 3.1.2, where each language name, written in that language, gets its own lang. "English" is not a Portuguese word, so none of the exceptions applies. The live page is unchanged.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the footer link "ENGLISH" to the English Carta de Serviços. The live HTML has no lang on it or on any ancestor except <html lang="pt-br">. It is an English word deliberately used as the language's own name, not a Portuguese loan word (Portuguese would say "Inglês"), and a pt-BR voice will mispronounce it. Exceptions that might rescue it: (1) Is it a proper name used across languages untranslated? No, it is translated in Portuguese. (2) Has it become vernacular? No. (3) Is the change of language unintended? No, it is clearly intended. None of these holds, so it fails 3.1.2.

ref: #body > header:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > a > img
subject: Selo comemorativo
message: The text alternative "Selo comemorativo" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header's 60-years seal (an SVG reading '60 anos') is the only content of a link to https://60anos.unicamp.br/ (titled 'Home - Unicamp 60 Anos'), and it opens in a new tab. Its alt is 'Selo comemorativo', so the link is announced as 'Selo comemorativo'. That doesn't give the text in the image ('60 anos') or the link's purpose (the site for Unicamp's 60th anniversary), and nothing in the link's programmatic context supplies it. Under H30/F89, a functional image must give the link's purpose, so this is a real 1.1.1 failure (and a 2.4.4 one). The live page still has the same markup.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The header seal image is the only content of a link to https://60anos.unicamp.br/ (opens the 60-years site in a new tab); the link has no aria-label or title, so its name is the alt "Selo comemorativo". The image visibly reads "60 anos", and the alt carries neither that text nor the destination, so a screen-reader user hears only 'commemorative seal' with no hint of the 60-years site. I looked for a reason it passes (a name on the link, a nearby text label, or an alt naming the anniversary) and found none on the live page. A functional image's alt must describe the link's purpose (H30), so this fails 1.1.1 as the finding says.

ref: #udum-secao-6acbfbfdda107 > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > img
subject: Placas de QR Code estão sendo afixadas nas árvores para proporcionar a pesquisadores e leigos uma observação mais apurada das plantas. Foto: Antonio Scarpinetti
message: The text alternative "Placas de QR Code estão sendo afixadas nas árvores para proporcionar a pesquisadores e leigos uma observação mais apurada das plantas. Foto: Antonio Scarpinetti" describes something the image does not show.
evidence: Placas de QR Code estão sendo afixadas nas árvores para proporcionar a pesquisadores e leigos uma observação mais apurada das plantas. Foto: Antonio Scarpinetti

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the cover-block background behind the grid of eight navigation links (Ingresso, Graduação, etc.). Its alt is a reused news caption: 'Placas de QR Code estão sendo afixadas nas árvores... Foto: Antonio Scarpinetti'. I opened the original image (man-po_arvores-unicamp_20220615_capa.jpg) and the screenshot. They show students walking along a tree-lined campus path, with no QR-code plates being put on trees. So the text alternative states content the image doesn't show and is not an equivalent, which fails 1.1.1 as the finding says. As a background behind links, the image is really decorative, so the proper fix is alt="". The suggested patch, which describes the button grid, is wrong, but that doesn't change the label.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the background image of the cover block behind the eight navigation tiles (Ingresso, Graduação, ...). I downloaded the full 1920x660 photo: it shows a tree-lined campus path with students walking, and no QR code plates are visible. The alt is a reused news caption about QR plates being attached to trees, plus a photo credit, so it describes an event the image does not show. If the image is informative, the alt is not equivalent. If it is decorative, which it is here, it should be alt="", and a non-null misleading alt fails 1.1.1 too (F39). The suggested patch is wrong: it describes the HTML buttons, not the photo. That does not change the label.

subject: E-mail
message: The placeholder "E-mail" has a contrast of 2.02:1 with the field (#b8b6b5 on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the newsletter e-mail field in the footer. It has no visible label: the placeholder 'E-mail' is the only on-screen text that tells users what to enter. I measured the screenshot pixels: the darkest placeholder glyph pixel is about #b8b7b7 on #ffffff, about 2.0:1, which matches Rampa's 2.02:1 and is far below the 4.5:1 that 14px/400 text needs. Placeholder text is text that carries information, so this fails 1.4.3. The live markup is unchanged.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the newsletter e-mail field in the footer. Its placeholder "E-mail" is the only visible label (the browser takes the accessible name from the placeholder). The theme CSS sets the .wpcf7 ::placeholder color to var(--background-primary-color) = #b8b6b5, on the field's white background. That computes to 2.02:1, confirmed in the screenshot, for 14px normal-weight text that needs 4.5:1. Placeholder text is not covered by any 1.4.3 exception (inactive component, decoration, logo), and here it is the field's only identifying text, so this fails 1.4.3.

ref: #gsc-i-id1
message: Nothing on screen tells what to enter in the field "pesquisar": its name is in aria-label, which only screen readers get.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the Google CSE search box in the header, in a 'search-compressed' container. When collapsed, the input is transparent (opacity 0, per the theme CSS) and is drawn as a magnifying-glass icon (the CSS ::before on .gsib_a), which the screenshot shows at the field's position. Clicking it expands the field and shows the visible label 'Buscar no site'. The Understanding document for 3.3.2 explicitly accepts a magnifying-glass icon as the visible label of a search field, so the claim that nothing on screen says what to enter is wrong. The icon is a CSS pseudo-element and doesn't appear in the snapshot the model judged. Separately, the field doesn't expand on keyboard focus and its outline is removed, which raises a possible 2.4.7 issue, not 3.3.2.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the Google CSE search input in the header, captured in its collapsed state: the input is transparent and a magnifying-glass icon (a CSS ::before on .gsib_a) shows where it is. The theme's all.min.js adds a <label for="gsc-i-id1">Buscar no site</label> after the input. When the box is clicked it gets .search-expand, and the CSS then displays that label as visible text above the field. The input also has title="pesquisar". So there is a visible text label when the field is in use, and the search icon labels it before then. The snapshot did not include either cue (the label is display:none in the collapsed state, and the icon is a pseudo-element), so 'nothing on screen tells what to enter' is not a fair reading of 3.3.2.

message: The icon of this link ("") has at most 2.56:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#00adee on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The first main-menu item is a link to https://www.fuvest.br showing only a FontAwesome home glyph (U+F015, 20px). The screenshot (sticky header) shows the light-blue icon on the white header bar; the snapshot records #00adee from CSS on #ffffff, which is 2.56:1. The icon is the only thing that identifies this control, so it is a graphical object required to understand it, and 1.4.11 requires 3:1 against adjacent colors (G207). It fails.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The home link in the main nav contains only a FontAwesome house glyph (U+F015, 20px). The header CSS (post-27095) sets nav items to #00adee on a section background of #ffffff, which is 2.56:1. The sticky header appears in the screenshot around y=6750, where the icon is the same light blue as the menu text. The glyph is the only thing that identifies the control, so 3:1 applies (G207), and it fails. Treated as text instead, it would fail 1.4.3 too. The high-contrast toggle does not qualify under G174.

ref: #menu-1-7478c58 > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
subject: link
message: The name the browser computes for this link is only an icon-font glyph (U+F015, a private use character from CSS), which screen readers do not read. Give it a text name (aria-label or visually hidden text) and hide the icon (aria-hidden).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The home link in the main menu (U+F015) has no aria-label, title or hidden text. Its name comes from its contents, which are only the private-use glyph U+F015: the snapshot's ax tree shows nameFrom contents, and the list item's name is \uf015. Screen readers announce nothing meaningful, so the link has no usable accessible name. It fails 4.1.2 (and 2.4.4). Minor inaccuracy: the glyph is literal DOM text styled with an icon font, not CSS-generated content, but the claim and the fix are right.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Live HTML: U+F015. It has no aria-label, title, visually hidden text, or img alt. The computed name is a single private-use code point, which screen readers do not voice, so the home link has no usable accessible name. It fails 4.1.2 (and 2.4.4). Nothing on the page gives it a name.

subject: Lula
message: The text alternative "Lula" is a file name or a placeholder.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is the photo of candidate Lula in the election results widget, with alt="Lula". That alt names the person shown, which is the right text alternative for a candidate photo. It is not a file name or a placeholder, even though the file is Lula.png. The "16%" in the crop is the end of the separate "45,16%" vote-bar text overlapping the photo, not part of the image. So the suggested alt "Lula com um selo de 16%" would be wrong.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the photo of candidate Lula in the election-results banner, with alt="Lula". The file is Lula.png, but the alt is the person's real name, which correctly identifies the photo (the visible text next to it repeats 'Lula PT 53.879.538 votos'). It is not a file name or placeholder in the F30 sense. The '16%' badge in the crop is the edge of the separate '45,16%' results bar drawn over the image bounds, not part of the image, so the suggested alt is also wrong. No 1.1.1 failure.

subject: Advertisement
message: The text alternative "Advertisement" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the Google Ad Manager banner (an Ágora/Bradesco ad). Its img is the only content of a link to the advertiser, with alt="Advertisement". The image is mostly text ("A evolução do seu jeito de investir", "Descubra uma nova experiência com o app Ágora", "Saiba mais"). "Advertisement" gives neither that text nor the link's purpose, so the functional image has no equivalent text alternative. That is a real 1.1.1 failure on the page (the ad is third-party and rotates, but it is part of the page as served). The link also fails 2.4.4.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Google ad (Ágora/Bradesco banner) inside the ad iframe: a link whose only content is an img with alt="Advertisement". The image holds the ad's text ('A evolução do seu jeito de investir... Saiba mais') and is the link's only content. The alt tells only that it is an ad, not the advertiser, message or destination. 1.1.1 requires a control's text alternative to describe its purpose, so this fails (also 2.4.4). Third-party ad content is not exempt from conformance. The ad creative may rotate on the live page.

message: The icon of this link has at most 1.97:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #22d467). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the WhatsApp channel link in the newsletter box: the WhatsApp brand logo (white glyph on WhatsApp green #22d467, on a #fbfbfb box). The 1.97:1 measurement is right, but the Understanding document for 1.4.11 exempts logos under the essential exception and says the exemption carries over to a UI component that is a logo. The logo is shown in its brand colours. Next to it is an "INSCREVA-SE" text link to the same WhatsApp URL. So this is not a 1.4.11 failure; at most it is the best-practice note in the Understanding document.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The link is the WhatsApp logo (icon-whatsapp.svg: white glyph on a green #22d467 circle, close to WhatsApp's brand green #25D366), linking to the Poder360 WhatsApp channel. Understanding 1.4.11 exempts logos under the essential exception, and says this exemption normatively carries over when a logo acts as a control. The brand colours are not an author choice to lower contrast. A separate, readable 'INSCREVA-SE' link right next to it goes to the same URL. Not a 1.4.11 failure.

ref: #page-885654 > div > div:nth-of-type(9) > form > fieldset > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > a
subject: INSCREVA-SE
message: The link text "INSCREVA-SE" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the green 'INSCREVA-SE' button in the 'alertas grátis do Poder360' box. Its accessible name is just 'Inscreva-se', and it goes to the Poder360 WhatsApp channel. The blue button next to it has the same name and goes to Telegram (t.me/Poder360). I checked the snapshot and the live HTML, which has not changed: the link has no aria-label, aria-labelledby, title or hidden text. The only thing that tells it apart is the WhatsApp icon, a separate link (img alt 'WhatsApp') in a sibling div. The two only share a generic div wrapper, not a sentence, paragraph, list item, table cell or associated header. So the context is not programmatically determined in the sense of G53/H77/H78/H79/H81, and a user on this link (in a links list, or tabbing) hears only 'Inscreva-se' and has to move focus to find out which channel it is. Sighted users get that from the icon and the colour, but that does not satisfy 2.4.4. The message's 'nothing around this one tells it apart' overstates it a little, since the adjacent icon does, but the failure it describes is real. The suggested fix ('Inscreva-se no canal do WhatsApp') would resolve it.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the green 'INSCREVA-SE' button (text 'Inscreva-se', uppercased by CSS) in the 'alertas grátis do Poder360' subscribe box. It links to the Poder360 WhatsApp channel. Its text is the same as the Telegram button's, which goes to t.me/Poder360. The only thing that tells it apart is the icon in the sibling div just before it: a separate <a> to the same URL whose img has alt "WhatsApp" (visible as the WhatsApp logo). I tried that as the reason it passes, and it does not hold. The icon and the button are in separate sibling divs (separate blocks), and the shared parent is a generic div. That is not the same sentence, paragraph, list item or table cell. The link has no aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby or title (the snapshot's ax data shows only name INSCREVA-SE), and the fieldset legend 'Formulário de cadastro' / label 'alertas grátis do Poder360' does not name the channel. To learn the channel, a screen-reader user has to leave the link and read the previous one. ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
subject: compartilhe
message: The icon of this link ("compartilhe") has at most 1.98:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #25d366). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the WhatsApp share link in the left share bar: a white WhatsApp glyph on a #25d366 circle (class 'green'). The ratio 1.98:1 is measured correctly. However, #25d366 with a white glyph is WhatsApp's own brand logo presentation. The 1.4.11 Understanding document places logos under the 'essential' exception and says the exemption carries over normatively when the logo is used as a user interface component. Giving it more contrast is only a best practice there. The low contrast comes from the brand colors, not from a design choice by this site, so this is not a 1.4.11 failure as WCAG defines it. The rule applied G207 without the logo exception.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: WhatsApp share link (aria-label 'compartilhe'): a white WhatsApp glyph in a 24px circle with background #25d366 (live CSS .article-share ... a.green). White on #25d366 is 1.98:1 (recomputed), and the green circle against the white page is also 1.98:1, so the control's only visual has low contrast. However, the glyph is the WhatsApp brand logo in its official colorway, and the 1.4.11 Understanding exempts logos (the essential exception). It only advises a higher-contrast variant when a logo acts as a UI component, and is not exempt when the low contrast is the author's choice. Auditors reasonably split on social-media brand icons, so this is not settled.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
subject: compartilhe
message: The link text "compartilhe" is shared by 3 links that lead to 3 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: All three links in this fixed share bar (Facebook, WhatsApp, Pinterest sharers) carry aria-label="compartilhe" and contain only an SVG brand icon with no title or name, so each link's accessible name is just "compartilhe" ('share'). The only programmatic context is the list/listitem and a sibling div reading "compartilhe", which names none of the services; the live page (checked 2026-10-11) has the same markup. Sighted users tell the links apart by the logos, but a screen-reader user hears three identical 'compartilhe' links that open three different services and cannot tell which is which, so the purpose of each link is not determinable from its text plus programmatic context, a 2.4.4 failure as the finding says (it is also arguably a 1.1.1 gap, since the label does not convey what the icon shows). This is the Facebook sharer link (icon-facebook); suggested name 'Compartilhar no Facebook' fits.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the first icon-only link in the fixed share bar beside the article. It opens the Facebook sharer and its only content is an SVG Facebook logo with no title. Its accessible name comes from aria-label="compartilhe" ("share"), which overrides the content. The WhatsApp and Pinterest links next to it have exactly the same name. I looked for a way it could pass and found none. The snapshot and the live HTML (unchanged on 2026-10-11) show no title, no aria-describedby and no visible or hidden text naming the network; the only context text is the visually hidden "compartilhe" in div.share-info. The exception for links ambiguous to users in general does not apply, because sighted users can see the brand icon. The Understanding document's remark that distinct link text is a "best practice" does not save it either: the network is part of what each link does, just as the format is in the Understanding document's PDF/mp3 example. A screen-reader user hears "compartilhe" three times and cannot pick a network. This fails 2.4.4 as claimed (the visual-only icon meaning also touches 1.1.1).

ref: #rodape > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > a
subject: Logotipo Hous 360
message: The icon of this link ("Logotipo Hous 360") has at most 2.21:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#abaeb9 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: This is the footer credit link to Hous360, the site's developer. Its only visible content is an SVG of the Hous logotype, with fill #575d73 inside a group set to opacity="0.5", so it renders about #abaeb9 on white. I computed 2.21:1, so the measurement is right, and the crop shows a faint grey logo. Logos and logotypes fall under 1.4.11's essential exception, and the Understanding document says that exemption normatively carries over to a control whose only content is a logo. But the same document says a logo that normally has enough contrast loses the exemption when an author chooses to show it with low contrast. Here #575d73 at full opacity would be about 6.5:1, and the 50% fade is hard-coded in the theme, but I cannot tell whether it comes from Hous360's brand guidelines. Competent auditors would reasonably split on this. The finding also calls the logo an "icon" (G207), which understates the logo question.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the footer "developed by" link to hous360.com.br. Its only visible content is an inline SVG logo whose paths are filled #575d73 inside <g opacity="0.5">. That renders exactly #abaeb9 on the white bar, about 2.2:1, matching the rule's measurement and the screenshot. The obvious defence is the logo exemption. However, the WCAG 2.2 Understanding for 1.4.11 says a logo presented at low contrast as an author choice, not because of brand colours, is not 'essential' and is not exempt. Here the brand colour #575d73 (about 6.5:1) is deliberately faded to 50% opacity, and no hover or focus style restores it (theme CSS checked). The logo is all that identifies the link, so it fails 1.4.11.

subject: Gaeilge
message: "Gaeilge" is in Irish, but it inherits the page's language (en): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="ga" to the link.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header navigation link 'Gaeilge' leads to the Irish-language site (index.ga.php). It is the name of the language written in Irish, and the live HTML has no lang attribute on it, so it inherits html lang="en". The Understanding document for 3.1.2 uses this exact case as its example ('Alternative language links': each language name, written in that language, carries a lang attribute). The language change is clearly intended, so the single-word and vernacular exceptions do not reasonably apply. This is a 3.1.2 failure.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the header language-switcher link "Gaeilge" (to the Irish version). Neither the link nor any ancestor has a lang attribute, so it inherits lang="en"; the live page is the same. Marking language-switcher endonyms with lang is common practice, and here a change of language is clearly intended. But the Understanding document for 3.1.2 exempts proper names, and a language's name arguably is one. It also says single words should be treated as part of the surrounding language unless a change is clearly intended. And 'Gaeilge' is in everyday Hiberno-English use; the site's own English text uses Irish terms such as 'Gaeltacht' unmarked. Competent auditors split on single-word language-switcher links, so I cannot call this a clear failure.

subject: heading|Northern lights Skies across the UK illu|The pink, green and purple hues of the n
message: “The pink, green and purple hues of the northern lights, vis…” shows under “Northern lights Skies across the UK illuminated by the nort…”, but the markup puts it before “Northern lights Skies across the UK illuminated by the nort…”, so a screen reader reads it as part of another section (flex-direction: column-reverse; WCAG 1.3.2, F1). Put the elements in the markup in the order they are meant to be read, and lay them out with CSS without reordering them.
evidence: on screen: “Northern lights Skies across the UK illuminated b…” → “The pink, green and purple hues of the northern l…”; read: “The pink, green and purple hues of the northern l…” → “Northern lights Skies across the UK illuminated b…”; flex-direction: column-reverse

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is a story card in a horizontal row of cards (Climate crisis & environment section). Inside one list item (whose overlay card link carries the headline as aria-label), a flex column with column-reverse holds the image (alt "The pink, green and purple hues of the northern lights, visible in...") first in the DOM and the h3 headline ("Northern lights Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights") second, so the headline shows above the photo but is read after its alt text. I checked the snapshot: both sit in the same li, the overlay card link (aria-label = headline) comes first, and every flagged card has this same structure. 1.3.2 and F1 only fail when the programmatic sequence changes the meaning; hearing a photo description just before the headline of the same card does not change what the card says, and the list item keeps it grouped with its own story, so the claim that it is read 'as part of another section' does not hold. Not a 1.3.2 failure: the rule treats any visual/DOM reorder as a failure regardless of meaning.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the flex column (column-reverse) inside one Guardian front card, first card of 'Climate crisis & environment'. In the DOM the card is: an empty overlay link whose aria-label is the headline ("Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights"), then the thumbnail img (alt "The pink, green and purple hues of the northern lights, vis…"), then the h3 kicker and headline; column-reverse only draws the headline above the thumbnail. The finding says the thumbnail is read as part of another section, but the snapshot shows the card's own headline link comes before the image in reading order, and image, link and heading all sit in the same li. So a screen reader reads headline link, photo, headline, all in the same card. Whether a thumbnail comes before or after its headline doesn't change what the card means, and 1.3.2 (and F1) apply only when the sequence affects meaning. The rule treats any DOM/visual mismatch across a heading as a failure, which is stricter than the criterion. The same pattern repeats on every card in these containers.

message: This passage has no lang attribute, so it is read as English (en), but it is in French (fr).

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The h3 card headline 'Henry Harris' recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme' (Food section) has no lang markup, so the French dish name is read with English rules. 3.1.2 exempts proper names and words that have become part of the surrounding vernacular. 'Tarte vaudoise à la crème' is not English vernacular, and a strict auditor would ask for lang="fr" on the multi-word French phrase. Many others treat a dish's name in an English recipe headline as a name, which needs no language change, and the passage is short and still understandable. The evidence does not settle which reading applies; competent auditors would reasonably disagree.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the h3 of a Food card, 'Dessert / Henry Harris’ recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme'. Neither the h3 nor any ancestor below <html lang="en"> has a lang attribute (the live page is the same), so a screen reader will say the French dish name with English rules. But 3.1.2 exempts proper names, technical terms and phrases that have entered the vernacular. A regional dish name in an English recipe headline ('tarte Vaudoise', capitalised as a name; 'à la crème' close to the naturalised 'à la carte') can be read as a culinary name/term rather than a passage in French. Competent auditors disagree on whether dish names like this need lang markup, so I can't settle it either way.

message: The field "Email Address:" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

auditor.label: true_positive

ref: #thomann-news > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > a:nth-of-type(1)
subject: YOUTUBE Marie Leloup plays Golden from "Kpop Demon Hunters" in the new Thomann Shop!
message: The link text "YOUTUBE Marie Leloup plays Golden from "Kpop Demon Hunters" in the new Thomann Shop!" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
evidence: YOUTUBE Marie Leloup plays Golden from "Kpop Demon Hunters" in the new Thomann Shop!

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the first 'Thomann News' teaser card. It links to youtube.com/watch?v=7aDSIaFjkXM, and its name is 'YouTube Marie Leloup plays Golden from "Kpop Demon Hunters" in the new Thomann Shop!'. The third card has the same name apart from the casing of 'KPop' and links to Bx3MLITMdtM. Both cards are still on the live page. I checked both videos: each is on Thomann's own channel, has exactly that title and the same description. 7aDSIaFjkXM is a 31-second Short, and Bx3MLITMdtM is the 3:15 full video of the same performance. So the link text is the exact title of the video it opens and correctly describes where the link goes. The Understanding document for 2.4.4 says the name of the destination is enough to describe the link's purpose. It lists different text for links with different destinations only as a best practice. Both links deliver the content they advertise: Marie Leloup playing Golden in the Thomann shop, on YouTube. The ACT definition of 'equivalent resource' allows the destinations to contain different amounts of information. The finding treats 'different URL' as 'different purpose' and applies the best practice as a requirement, which is closer to 2.4.9 (AAA). This is a borderline call. The thumbnails differ visually (a vertical clip with blurred sides versus a 'VIOLIN COVER' title card), they are presentational (alt=""), and the proposed ACT rule fd3a94 could be read as failing an excerpt-versus-full pair. Even so, sighted users get no more information than screen-reader users about which card is the Short and which is the full video. Rampa never read the destinations.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the first 'Thomann News' teaser card, a link to youtube.com/watch?v=7aDSIaFjkXM named 'YouTube Marie Leloup plays Golden from "Kpop Demon Hunters" in the new Thomann Shop!'. The third card (Bx3MLITMdtM) has the same name apart from letter case. The finding's facts are right: the names match, the URLs differ, and no programmatic context sets them apart. But Rampa never read the destinations. Both are Thomann Music videos with exactly these titles and the same description, showing the same performance: the first is a 31-second Short and the second the full 195-second video. Each link's text is the title of the video it opens, which Understanding 2.4.4 calls sufficient to describe a link's purpose. That document lists different text for different destinations only as a best practice. The ACT rule for 2.4.4 (fd3a94, still only proposed) passes links that lead to equivalent resources. Its definition says such resources may differ in how much information they hold, so long as the key content they advertise (this performance) is the same. A user can tell what either link does. The only thing the text does not reveal is which one is the short clip, and the visible text does not tell sighted users that either. Some auditors would still flag the duplicate as a 2.4.4 problem. The thumbnails' empty alt text is a separate question, not this claim. The live page still had both links on 2026-10-11.

auditor.rationale: The <title> 'Keep me informed' is the same as the H1 and states the page's purpose: signing up to be kept informed, that is, the newsletter. WCAG 2.4.2 asks for a title that describes the topic or purpose. It does not require the site name, although adding 'Rijksmuseum' or 'newsletter' would help. The claim that the title 'says nothing about this page' is not accurate. This is not a 2.4.2 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The document title is 'Keep me informed', identical to the page's h1, on a page whose sole content is a newsletter sign-up ('Sign me up for the general English newsletter'). The title states the page's purpose, which is what 2.4.2 asks; it lacks the site name, but WCAG does not require one (adding it is advisory). The finding's claim that it 'says nothing about this page' does not hold; the suggested 'Newsletter Sign-up - Rijksmuseum' is a best-practice improvement, not a fix for a failure.

subject: Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)

evidence: Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is a 32px vehicle icon inside the 'Mais Acessados' link to service 2671. The link also shows the same text, 'Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)', and the live HTML is unchanged. An image inside a link may take an alt that states the link's function, so 1.1.1 does not require the alt to describe the picture. The alt only repeats the visible text. alt="" would be better practice (H2), but that redundancy is not a 1.1.1 failure. The suggested 'Ícone de veículo' would add nothing useful.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is a 32x32 vehicle pictogram inside the 'Mais Acessados' link whose visible text is 'Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)'. Its alt names the service the icon stands for, which is a functional or symbolic alternative, and WCAG 1.1.1 asks for equivalent purpose, not a description of how the icon looks. The alt repeats the adjacent link text. That is a redundancy issue (H2 or alt="" would be cleaner), but it is not a 1.1.1 failure, and it is not the mismatch the finding claims. The suggested patch, 'Ícone de veículo', would make it worse. The live markup is unchanged.

ref: #cc-for-you > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > img
subject: Ceará em Destaque
message: The text alternative "Ceará em Destaque" describes something the image does not show.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the featured photo of the 'Ceará em Destaque' bulletin card (a buggy on a sand dune). It is not inside a link, and the h3 directly above it is also 'Ceará em Destaque'. The alt names the publication, not what the photo shows, and the live HTML is the same. If the photo is treated as informative, the alt does not convey its content and the finding holds. If it is an illustration in a card whose information is all in the heading, date and link, it is decorative and the alt is only redundant. That would be at most an F38-style issue, not the inaccurate description the finding claims. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree about whether this photo carries information.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the featured photo of the 'Ceará em Destaque' bulletin card: a buggy on a dune with a beach behind it. It sits directly under the h3 'Ceará em Destaque' and above 'Boletim publicado! 09/10/2026 / Ler boletim'. The image is not a link, and its alt repeats the h3. Competent auditors would split three ways. One reading treats it as an informative photo, so the alt fails as claimed. Another treats it as ambience next to its own heading, in which case the right fix is alt="" (an F38-style issue) rather than a description. A third treats it as the edition's cover image, which is fairly identified by the publication's title. The evidence cannot settle which purpose the photo serves.

ref: #login-button-desktop
subject: Entrar
message: The text "Entrar" has at most 3.42:1 contrast with what is behind it (#fefefe on #22a33e…#1e9f41), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a gradient). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the desktop 'Entrar' outline button in the header: white text on the header's green gradient. Sampling the screenshot inside the button gives #21a23e to #24a53a behind #fefefe, about 3.2:1 to 3.4:1. At 20px and weight 400 the text is not large, so it needs 4.5:1, and it fails. The page has an 'Alternar alto contraste' toggle, but G174 does not rescue this. G174 requires the alternate presentation to meet all other criteria, and that mode would keep failures such as the file-name alt on the 'Especiais' banner. So 1.4.3 fails in the default view.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The measurement holds up. The 'Entrar' link in the header is #fefefe text on the green header gradient (about #20a13f behind it). style.css sets .btn-outline-cc to 1.25rem (20px) with font-weight 400 !important, so this is normal-size text needing 4.5:1, and it reaches only about 3.3-3.5:1 in the default presentation. The page, however, offers a visible, focusable 'Ativar alto contraste' toggle in the same header (its icon is about 3.8:1 against the green; it is also bound to Alt+Shift+C). Activating it sets body.contrast-active, and menu-mobile.css then forces the header to #111 with white text, which passes. This is technique G174. Whether that suffices is debatable: G174 needs the control itself to meet the contrast requirement, and it is an icon at 3.8:1, not text at 4.5:1. It also needs the alternate version to conform fully, which this page's other failures make doubtful. Auditors would reasonably disagree, so this is a true positive only if the toggle is not accepted.

ref: #gsc-i-id1
message: Nothing on screen tells what to enter in the field "pesquisar": its name is in aria-label, which only screen readers get.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the Google CSE search box in the header, in a 'search-compressed' container. When collapsed, the input is transparent (opacity 0, per the theme CSS) and is drawn as a magnifying-glass icon (the CSS ::before on .gsib_a), which the screenshot shows at the field's position. Clicking it expands the field and shows the visible label 'Buscar no site'. The Understanding document for 3.3.2 explicitly accepts a magnifying-glass icon as the visible label of a search field, so the claim that nothing on screen says what to enter is wrong. The icon is a CSS pseudo-element and doesn't appear in the snapshot the model judged. Separately, the field doesn't expand on keyboard focus and its outline is removed, which raises a possible 2.4.7 issue, not 3.3.2.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the Google CSE search input in the header, captured in its collapsed state: the input is transparent and a magnifying-glass icon (a CSS ::before on .gsib_a) shows where it is. The theme's all.min.js adds a <label for="gsc-i-id1">Buscar no site</label> after the input. When the box is clicked it gets .search-expand, and the CSS then displays that label as visible text above the field. The input also has title="pesquisar". So there is a visible text label when the field is in use, and the search icon labels it before then. The snapshot did not include either cue (the label is display:none in the collapsed state, and the icon is a pseudo-element), so 'nothing on screen tells what to enter' is not a fair reading of 3.3.2.

It is visible text with no 1.4.3 exception (the control is active), so it fails 1.4.3.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Placeholder 'Digite seu email' of the footer newsletter email field. Live CSS: .input::placeholder {color: var(--gray-50)} = #a3a3a3 on a white field, 14px weight 400: 2.52:1, below 4.5:1, matching the snapshot. Possible objection: placeholders are not required to meet contrast. That does not hold here. 1.4.3 has no placeholder exception, the field is not inactive, and the placeholder is the field's only visible label and its accessible name, so it is information users need.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
subject: compartilhe
message: The icon of this link ("compartilhe") has at most 1.98:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #25d366). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the WhatsApp share link in the left share bar: a white WhatsApp glyph on a #25d366 circle (class 'green'). The ratio 1.98:1 is measured correctly. However, #25d366 with a white glyph is WhatsApp's own brand logo presentation. The 1.4.11 Understanding document places logos under the 'essential' exception and says the exemption carries over normatively when the logo is used as a user interface component. Giving it more contrast is only a best practice there. The low contrast comes from the brand colors, not from a design choice by this site, so this is not a 1.4.11 failure as WCAG defines it. The rule applied G207 without the logo exception.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: WhatsApp share link (aria-label 'compartilhe'): a white WhatsApp glyph in a 24px circle with background #25d366 (live CSS .article-share ... a.green). White on #25d366 is 1.98:1 (recomputed), and the green circle against the white page is also 1.98:1, so the control's only visual has low contrast. However, the glyph is the WhatsApp brand logo in its official colorway, and the 1.4.11 Understanding exempts logos (the essential exception). It only advises a higher-contrast variant when a logo acts as a UI component, and is not exempt when the low contrast is the author's choice. Auditors reasonably split on social-media brand icons, so this is not settled.

ref: #header > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > label
subject: LabelText click,keydown
message: This element ("Busca IA do Tua Saúde") takes keyboard focus and listens to click, keydown, so it works as a control, but the browser exposes it as LabelText, with no control role: a screen reader does not announce it as a button or a link (F59). Use the native element (button, a) or give it the role of the control it is.
evidence: role LabelText · click, keydown · "Busca IA do Tua Saúde"

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header 'Busca IA do Tua Saúde' trigger is a <label for=headerSearch tabindex=0> with click and keydown listeners. The input it points to sits inside a hidden search container, so this label is the only way to open the search overlay. Chrome exposes it as LabelText with an empty computed name and no button or link role. Native labels do not respond to Enter, so the keyboard behavior is scripted. This is a scripted custom control whose role is not programmatically determinable (F59 pattern), so 4.1.2 fails. A <button> or role=button would fix it.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Header '<label tabindex="0" for="headerSearch" class="search">Busca IA do Tua Saúde</label>'. The snapshot shows the real search form container (.header-tuasaude-search-container) hidden, so this focusable label, with click and keydown listeners, is the visible trigger that opens the AI search. Chrome exposes it as LabelText with no control role and an empty name of its own. A screen reader user who reaches it hears only text, not a button. Its native label behavior (focusing #headerSearch) cannot be what makes it work while that input is hidden. A scripted, focusable control with no role is the F59 pattern, so it fails 4.1.2 as reported.

ref: #rodape > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > a
subject: Logotipo Hous 360
message: The icon of this link ("Logotipo Hous 360") has at most 2.21:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#abaeb9 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: This is the footer credit link to Hous360, the site's developer. Its only visible content is an SVG of the Hous logotype, with fill #575d73 inside a group set to opacity="0.5", so it renders about #abaeb9 on white. I computed 2.21:1, so the measurement is right, and the crop shows a faint grey logo. Logos and logotypes fall under 1.4.11's essential exception, and the Understanding document says that exemption normatively carries over to a control whose only content is a logo. But the same document says a logo that normally has enough contrast loses the exemption when an author chooses to show it with low contrast. Here #575d73 at full opacity would be about 6.5:1, and the 50% fade is hard-coded in the theme, but I cannot tell whether it comes from Hous360's brand guidelines. Competent auditors would reasonably split on this. The finding also calls the logo an "icon" (G207), which understates the logo question.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the footer "developed by" link to hous360.com.br. Its only visible content is an inline SVG logo whose paths are filled #575d73 inside <g opacity="0.5">. That renders exactly #abaeb9 on the white bar, about 2.2:1, matching the rule's measurement and the screenshot. The obvious defence is the logo exemption. However, the WCAG 2.2 Understanding for 1.4.11 says a logo presented at low contrast as an author choice, not because of brand colours, is not 'essential' and is not exempt. Here the brand colour #575d73 (about 6.5:1) is deliberately faded to 50% opacity, and no hover or focus style restores it (theme CSS checked). The logo is all that identifies the link, so it fails 1.4.11.

skeptic.label: false_positive

Link text together with its enclosing sentence or list item is programmatically determined context (G53, H78/H79-style context), so the purpose is clear. The URL also names the operator's contact page. WCAG 2.4.4 does not forbid a URL as link text. Rejecting it as "an address, not a purpose" applies a stricter rule than the criterion. ref: html > body > header > div > div > div > div > nav > ul > li:nth-of-type(7) > a
subject: Gaeilge
message: "Gaeilge" is in Irish, but it inherits the page's language (en): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="ga" to the link.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header navigation link 'Gaeilge' leads to the Irish-language site (index.ga.php). It is the name of the language written in Irish, and the live HTML has no lang attribute on it, so it inherits html lang="en". The Understanding document for 3.1.2 uses this exact case as its example ('Alternative language links': each language name, written in that language, carries a lang attribute). The language change is clearly intended, so the single-word and vernacular exceptions do not reasonably apply. This is a 3.1.2 failure.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the header language-switcher link "Gaeilge" (to the Irish version). Neither the link nor any ancestor has a lang attribute, so it inherits lang="en"; the live page is the same. Marking language-switcher endonyms with lang is common practice, and here a change of language is clearly intended. But the Understanding document for 3.1.2 exempts proper names, and a language's name arguably is one. It also says single words should be treated as part of the surrounding language unless a change is clearly intended. And 'Gaeilge' is in everyday Hiberno-English use; the site's own English text uses Irish terms such as 'Gaeltacht' unmarked. Competent auditors split on single-word language-switcher links, so I cannot call this a clear failure.

subject: heading|Northern lights Skies across the UK illu|The pink, green and purple hues of the n
message: “The pink, green and purple hues of the northern lights, vis…” shows under “Northern lights Skies across the UK illuminated by the nort…”, but the markup puts it before “Northern lights Skies across the UK illuminated by the nort…”, so a screen reader reads it as part of another section (flex-direction: column-reverse; WCAG 1.3.2, F1). Put the elements in the markup in the order they are meant to be read, and lay them out with CSS without reordering them.
evidence: on screen: “Northern lights Skies across the UK illuminated b…” → “The pink, green and purple hues of the northern l…”; read: “The pink, green and purple hues of the northern l…” → “Northern lights Skies across the UK illuminated b…”; flex-direction: column-reverse

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is a story card in a horizontal row of cards (Climate crisis & environment section). Inside one list item (whose overlay card link carries the headline as aria-label), a flex column with column-reverse holds the image (alt "The pink, green and purple hues of the northern lights, visible in...") first in the DOM and the h3 headline ("Northern lights Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights") second, so the headline shows above the photo but is read after its alt text. I checked the snapshot: both sit in the same li, the overlay card link (aria-label = headline) comes first, and every flagged card has this same structure. 1.3.2 and F1 only fail when the programmatic sequence changes the meaning; hearing a photo description just before the headline of the same card does not change what the card says, and the list item keeps it grouped with its own story, so the claim that it is read 'as part of another section' does not hold. Not a 1.3.2 failure: the rule treats any visual/DOM reorder as a failure regardless of meaning.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the flex column (column-reverse) inside one Guardian front card, first card of 'Climate crisis & environment'. In the DOM the card is: an empty overlay link whose aria-label is the headline ("Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights"), then the thumbnail img (alt "The pink, green and purple hues of the northern lights, vis…"), then the h3 kicker and headline; column-reverse only draws the headline above the thumbnail. The finding says the thumbnail is read as part of another section, but the snapshot shows the card's own headline link comes before the image in reading order, and image, link and heading all sit in the same li. So a screen reader reads headline link, photo, headline, all in the same card. Whether a thumbnail comes before or after its headline doesn't change what the card means, and 1.3.2 (and F1) apply only when the sequence affects meaning. The rule treats any DOM/visual mismatch across a heading as a failure, which is stricter than the criterion. The same pattern repeats on every card in these containers.

ref: #container-food > gu-island > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > h3
subject: unmarked|en|tarte Vaudoise à la creme
message: This passage has no lang attribute, so it is read as English (en), but it is in French (fr).

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The h3 card headline 'Henry Harris' recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme' (Food section) has no lang markup, so the French dish name is read with English rules. 3.1.2 exempts proper names and words that have become part of the surrounding vernacular. 'Tarte vaudoise à la crème' is not English vernacular, and a strict auditor would ask for lang="fr" on the multi-word French phrase. Many others treat a dish's name in an English recipe headline as a name, which needs no language change, and the passage is short and still understandable. The evidence does not settle which reading applies; competent auditors would reasonably disagree.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the h3 of a Food card, 'Dessert / Henry Harris’ recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme'. Neither the h3 nor any ancestor below <html lang="en"> has a lang attribute (the live page is the same), so a screen reader will say the French dish name with English rules. But 3.1.2 exempts proper names, technical terms and phrases that have entered the vernacular. A regional dish name in an English recipe headline ('tarte Vaudoise', capitalised as a name; 'à la crème' close to the naturalised 'à la carte') can be read as a culinary name/term rather than a passage in French. Competent auditors disagree on whether dish names like this need lang markup, so I can't settle it either way.

ref: #newsletter-signup-email-1
message: The field "Email Address:" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the footer newsletter sign-up field, an input type="email" with a visually hidden label "Email Address:". It collects the user's own email address, which is one of the WCAG input purposes. The snapshot has no autocomplete attribute anywhere on the page. The live HTML fetched on 2026-10-11 has the same markup (only the id suffix differs) and still no autocomplete. type="email" gives the data type, not the input purpose, so nothing makes the purpose programmatically determinable. That fails 1.3.5 as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the footer newsletter sign-up input (type=email, name=email, a visually hidden label 'Email Address:', posts to signup.propublica.org). It asks for the user's own email address, which is an input purpose listed in WCAG 1.3.5. The snapshot and the live HTML fetched on 2026-10-11 both show no autocomplete attribute, and Chromium flagged the same thing. type=email only sets the data format and does not identify the purpose, and no ARIA or other mechanism does either. I looked for a reason it passes (for example, the address belonging to someone else, or autocomplete being added by script) and found none. Fails 1.3.5.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the email input in the bottom-panel newsletter CTA ('Get the Newsletter'), with type=email, name=email and placeholder you@example.com. It collects the user's own email address, but neither the snapshot nor the live HTML has autocomplete=email, and Chromium's form check flagged it. type=email does not identify the purpose under 1.3.5, the sufficient technique is H98 (autocomplete), and nothing else on the element supplies the purpose. The claim holds.

The finding's wording is loose (the real gap is the missing "30", not invented content), but its claim of an alt/image mismatch holds, and its patch "30 Days Money-Back" names the fix. ref: html > body > header:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a
subject: Español
message: "Español" is in Spanish, but it inherits the page's language (en-us): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="es" to the link.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the "Español" language-switcher link in the top official-notice banner, pointing to https://www.cdc.gov/spanish/. The snapshot shows <html lang="en-us"> and no lang attribute on the link or any of its ancestors, so the Spanish word is exposed as English. A language name in its own language is not a proper name or vernacular term under the 3.1.2 exceptions. The 3.1.2 Understanding document's own language-switcher example says each link's language is indicated with a lang attribute, and it shows Español marked with lang="es". skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the header link "Español" to the Spanish CDC site. The snapshot has exactly one lang attribute on the whole page, lang="en-us" on <html>. Neither the link nor any wrapper marks it as Spanish, and the live page shows the same markup. The Understanding document for 3.1.2 uses this exact case as its example: alternative-language links whose text is the language's name in that language need a lang attribute, and it shows "Español" with lang="es". None of the exceptions apply: the word is not a proper name, a technical term or English vernacular, and the change of language is clearly intended. The other "Español" links on the page have the same problem, but this finding names a real failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive

subject: Keep me informed
message: The page title "Keep me informed" says nothing about this page.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The <title> 'Keep me informed' is the same as the H1 and states the page's purpose: signing up to be kept informed, that is, the newsletter. WCAG 2.4.2 asks for a title that describes the topic or purpose. It does not require the site name, although adding 'Rijksmuseum' or 'newsletter' would help. The claim that the title 'says nothing about this page' is not accurate. This is not a 2.4.2 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The document title is 'Keep me informed', identical to the page's h1, on a page whose sole content is a newsletter sign-up ('Sign me up for the general English newsletter'). The title states the page's purpose, which is what 2.4.2 asks; it lacks the site name, but WCAG does not require one (adding it is advisory). The finding's claim that it 'says nothing about this page' does not hold; the suggested 'Newsletter Sign-up - Rijksmuseum' is a best-practice improvement, not a fix for a failure.
